I Ran an App Store PPO Experiment on My Icon

A practical icon A/B test using Apple’s Product Page Optimization — and what I learned.

January 24, 2026

I’ve spent an embarrassing amount of time tweaking the “big” things in my app - features, onboarding, performance — and this was all useful stuff for driving up conversion rates. But for easily two years I treated the App Store icon like a set-and-forget detail.

I was even sucked into Marc Lou's LogoFast tool that makes it easy to generate an app icon in literally minutes. At the time I didn't particularly bother what it looked like as I was so focussed on the app itself.

Then I realised something annoying but true: for most people, your icon is the first impression. Literally before they read a word of your description, before they see your screenshots, they see a tiny square and make a snap judgement.

So I finally did the responsible thing and ran a real test using Apple’s Product Page Optimization (PPO) — basically App Store A/B testing — to start trialing different icons and finding which one converted the best. Below are the results of just one of these tests.

The Setup: What I Tested

PPO lets you create up to 3 treatments and split traffic between them. I kept it simple: one control (my current icon) vs one variant (the new icon).

Success metric: Product Page Views → Downloads (i.e. conversion rate).
Audience: All traffic with a split of 50%
Duration: 14 days

The Results

Here’s the outcome. I’m sharing both the headline numbers and the day-by-day trend, because PPO results can wobble a lot with traffic quality, day-of-week effects, and random variance.

Headline: Variant was +3.32% compared to control.
Control conversion: 11.78%
Variant conversion: 12.17%
Installs: Control X, Variant X
Confidence: Inconclusive (1.1% confidence!)

What I Learned (So You Don’t Have To)

A few takeaways that surprised me:

  • Small visual changes can beat big feature work — if you’re bottlenecked on conversion.
  • Early results are noisy — I saw swings that looked “real” and then completely reverted.
  • Traffic source matters — browse vs search vs ads can behave differently.
  • Don’t overfit — an icon can “win” for the wrong reasons if the sample is tiny.

How To Run Your Own PPO Icon Test

If you’re an indie dev, this is the most straightforward way to do it:

  1. Create one strong alternative icon (don’t test 5 tiny tweaks at once).
  2. Set up PPO with a simple Control vs Variant split.
  3. Run it long enough to reduce day-to-day randomness (especially over a weekend).
  4. Export results and look at both the headline and the trend.
  5. Only ship the winner if it’s meaningful and stable.

Conclusion

PPO is one of those rare platform features that’s genuinely helpful for indies: it lets you make decisions with data instead of vibes. Even if your test is inconclusive, you’ll learn faster than you would by shipping random icon changes and guessing.

Next up, I’m planning to test (screenshots / preview video / subtitle — pick one). If you want, I’ll share the template I use to export + chart results too.
